evidence: Plin. NH 24.90: rhododaphnēn vocant aut nērium
terms.comment: Greek νήριον. Pliny says that the Greek rhododendros had found no Latin name, and that it was called rhododaphnē or nērium (NH 24.90): we put first the shorter word, which Linnaeus kept for the genus (Nerium oleander). Lewis & Short heads it nērion, with nērium beside it; Pliny’s text has nērium. He says the leaves are poison to cattle, goats, and sheep (NH 16.79; 24.90). The later Latin oleander is in none of Lewis & Short, Traupman, Morgan–Owens, Levi–Bini, or Andresian.
Also feminine, rhododendros (NH 24.90). Botanists now give the name to another genus, Rhododendron.

phrases.latin: rhododendron, ut nōmine appāret, ā Graecīs venit. aliī nērium vocārunt, aliī rhododaphnēn, sempiternum fronde, rosae similitūdine, caulibus fruticōsum.
phrases.english: The rhododendron, as its name shows, came from the Greeks. Some have called it nerium, others rhododaphne: evergreen in its leaves, like the rose to look at, shrubby in its stems.

phrases.latin: Rhododendros nē nōmen quidem apud nōs invēnit Latīnum; rhododaphnēn vocant aut nērium.
phrases.english: The rhododendros has not even found a Latin name among us; they call it rhododaphne or nerium.

sources: Lewis & Short: nerion · Lewis & Short: rhododaphne · Lewis & Short: rhododendros
